newsitem.title: UK: Coffee, nickel and zinc are among 1997 winners so far.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, nickel and zinc are among 1997 winners so far.

text.p: Prices for coffee and some of the industrial metals, notably nickel and zinc, ended January sharply up from end-1996 levels but gold was a loser in volatile commodity markets, down almost seven percent in the month.

Crude oil was easier that at the start of January although it remains firm and not too far below the post-Gulf War highs to which it was driven by low stocks and strong winter demand for heating fuel in North America and Europe .
London Robusta coffee futures rose as high as $1,595 per tonne this week on fund-led buying, compared with $1,235 at the end of 1996.

Low stocks were a factor in coffee, too. An accord on new export curbs by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries and prospects of a lower-than-expected Brazil crop also buoyed this market and encouraged the speculative buying.

Prices ended the week off Wednesday's highs down at $1,500 on the March Robusta contract after speculators and producers sold to lock in their gains, but traders saw potential for another rally on any news to confirm that supply is tight.
Nickel prices stood at around $7,600 per tonne on Friday on the London Metal Exchange. This was up by 18-1/2 percent during the month. Zinc was firmer by 10 percent at $1,170.
Dealers said funds were buyers of both these metals in markets characterized by tight stocks and brisk demand.
The price of gold skidded to fresh 3-1/4 year lows on Friday, in a market that dealers said was wracked by widespread speculation about new central bank selling.
Bullion was fixed at $345 an ounce in the London morning level, lowest since September 14, 1993, and down a dramatic $4.25 from Thursday.

Fresh rumours of central bank sales, just weeks after the Dutch central bank announced it had sold 300 tonnes from its reserves, injected a chill into the already nervous market, several dealers said.
The market has been on edge watching gold plunge nearly seven percent since the start of 1997. Prices are also down some 17 percent since a rally peaked at $417 almost exactly a year ago.
After the rally subsided, gold lost favour with investors in favour of booming stock and bond markets in recent months.
Crude oil and wheat prices ended January just easier from the start of 1997.
